source.title: Estimating the Effects of Sample Training Orders for Large Language Models without Retraining
source.authors: Hao Yang; Hao-Xuan Li; Mengyue Yang; Xu Chen; Ming-Ming Gong

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices and limitations.
record.tranche_reason: The paper estimates and validates training-order effects on memorization and generalization in a language model, a new setting relative to the listed versions; it also reports results directly relevant to V8's training-example influence claim, but does not remove examples.
record.gate_note: The study varies training-batch order and estimates its effect on perplexity for training batches and unseen data. Rows below capture reported training-order outcomes bearing on memorization/generalization; curriculum comparisons and estimator-accuracy results do not directly test a listed version and are not included.
record.test_reason: Table 2 bears on V5: the same WikiText-103 training set is divided into different numbers of batches, training lasts one epoch, and actual held-out perplexity is reported. Appendix B.1.3 confirms that gradient accumulation implements the larger batches. Across every curriculum strategy, T=8 (larger batches) has worse perplexity than T=256 (smaller batches). The training-order findings themselves test none of V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors present FUT as an efficient estimator of performance under alternative training orders, demonstrate curriculum selection, and report position-dependent memorization and similarity-dependent generalization. Their validation uses perplexity; they explicitly leave validation on downstream understanding and reasoning tasks for future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sample-order permutation and estimated perplexity in a 636 million-parameter language model; the listed versions concern label memorization, architecture, optimization, regularization, sharpness, or example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect on generalization differs by training-batch similarity to D: similar batches show better generalization when placed later, while dissimilar batches have little or random effect. Training position is varied.

fits_no_version.finding: Later training positions generally yield lower perplexity on the training batch itself.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this single-epoch language-model setting, later exposure improves retention of a training batch relative to earlier exposure.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that later placement improves unseen-data perplexity for similar batches, whereas dissimilar batches show little or irregular position dependence. Individual batch-to-group assignments in the record require correction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of training-batch position on unseen-data perplexity depends on similarity between the batch and evaluation data.

record.problems: The memorization/generalization analysis uses a single 636 million-parameter LLaMA-architecture model and T=8. Outcomes are displayed in figures without numerical values in the text. The authors say the analysis evaluates generalization using perplexity only and that further validation on complex downstream tasks is needed. FUT uses Taylor approximations and random projection, which may introduce approximation error.
record.rows_left_out: Rows from Sections 5.1 and 5.2 and Appendix C about estimator accuracy, runtime, curriculum-search comparisons, model-scale estimation, and intermediate-step estimates were omitted because they concern the proposed estimation method or curriculum performance, not a version's named claim. No results were extracted from the cited prior work.

untested.parts: No comparison of fixed random labels with natural labels, training fit, or chance-level held-out performance.
No width sweep establishing zero training error and subsequent test-error behavior.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
Adam is used without an SGD or momentum-SGD comparison.

No longer-training intervention, warmup or learning-rate-scaling comparison, normalization or regularization intervention, or demonstration that an adapted recipe eliminates the batch penalty. The workload-dependent threshold is not established.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements, generalization-gap rankings, or comparison with norm and margin measures.
No inclusion-based memorization scores or removal-and-retraining comparison against equally many random examples. Training position is a different intervention.

missing.what: Add actual held-out perplexity comparisons across batch numbers from Table 2, linked to V5. Although rows_left_out declares curriculum results omitted, excluding all of them overlooks the fixed-epoch batch-size comparison. For random order, T=8,16,32,64,128,256 gives 1.4414,1.4599,1.4109,1.4248,1.3838,1.3696. Record actual results separately from parenthesized estimator predictions.

record.verdict_notes: The batch-size evidence is incidental to the paper's estimator and curriculum objectives but still bears on V5. Table 1 reports estimation error and cannot establish a generalization penalty. Table 2 reports actual perplexities and can. Existing row states are changed to cannot_determine relative to the listed versions; this does not deny the authors' separate training-order findings. Figures 4–5 do not justify duplicating nearly every batch into both similarity groups for the same evaluation dataset.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting random labels with generalizing on natural labels.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer comparison.
Does not compare large and small batch sizes for generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
Does not remove and retrain after removing memorized examples; it varies the position of a batch in the training order.

rows.value: Figure 3 reports FUT, FUT++, and retraining heatmap values; exact values are not stated in text.
rows.note: Authors state that the model tends to memorize batches appearing later more effectively, as indicated by lower perplexity; the figure's individual values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Training-batch perplexity under reordered training does not measure any listed version's effect. Figure 3 covers all eight selected batches, not only B0. Numerical heatmap entries are present in the supplied text, although their spatial alignment is difficult to recover.

relationships.condition: 636M-parameter LLaMA architecture on WikiText-103, one training epoch, comparing T=8 larger batches with T=256 smaller batches across the six Table 2 curricula.
relationships.reason: Based on Table 2 rather than existing rows: actual perplexity is higher with larger batches for every curriculum; random order gives 1.4414 versus 1.3696, and FUT++ gives 1.3998 versus 1.3178. These are trained-model results, not the parenthesized estimates.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports higher trained-model perplexity with larger batches across every tested curriculum after one epoch, but these comparisons remain unverified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
